stem: Muhammad Ghori granted first Iqta in India to –
expl: Soon after Ghori’s victories, the Iqta system was established in North India. In India, Muhammad Ghori granted the first Iqta to Qutbuddin Aibak. From 1192 to 1206 AD, Aibak administered the conquered parts of North India as Ghori’s representative. During this period, Aibak also expanded Turkish power in North India.

stem: Muhammad Ghori was defeated by the Chaulukyas of Gujarat in

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: Muhammad Ghori attacked Gujarat in 1178 AD. At that time, the Anhilwad Chalukya ruler of Gujarat was Mularaja II. Naika Devi, the widowed mother of Mularaja II, acted as his guardian and led the Chalukya (Solanki) army against Ghori. Near Mount Abu, on the field of Kasahrada, the Chalukya/ Solanki army defeated Muhammad Ghori. This was Ghori’s first defeat in India. Some sources also mention this invasion (1178 AD) during the reign of Bhima II. This confusion probably arises because Mularaja II’s reign ended in 1178 AD and Bhima II’s reign began in the same year. However, most historians accept Mularaja II as the Chalukya/Solanki ruler of Gujarat at the time of Ghori’s invasion (1178 AD).

stem: Who was the first ruler of the Slave Dynasty?
expl: The first ruler of the Slave Dynasty in India was Qutbuddin Aibak (1206–1210 AD). He belonged to a Turkish tribe called Aibak. In childhood, he was purchased as a slave by Qazi Fakhruddin Abdul Aziz Kufi of Nishapur. The Qazi took proper care of him and ensured that he received complete education. Aibak recited the Quran in a very melodious voice; therefore, he became famous as Quran-khwan (one who recites the Quran). Later, he was brought from Nishapur to Ghazni, where Ghori purchased him. Due to his talent, dedication, and honesty, Aibak soon gained Ghori’s trust. Ghori promoted him to the post of Amir-e-Akhur, and from there a new chapter of his life began. He was the first Turkish ruler of Delhi, although he ruled from Lahore. Aibak never formally assumed the title of Sultan. He remained content with the titles of Malik and Sipahsalar. After receiving a deed of manumission from Ghiyasuddin, Ghori’s successor, Aibak was officially freed from slavery in 1208 AD.

stem: The capital of Qutbuddin Aibak was:
expl: After the death of Muhammad Ghori (1206 AD), the notable people and amirs of Lahore invited Qutb-ud-din Aibak to assume sovereign powers. Therefore, he went to Lahore, assumed power, and was formally enthroned in 1206 AD. Aibak’s capital was Lahore. After ascending the throne, Aibak’s biggest challenge came from Taj-ud-din Yalduz and Nasir-ud-din Qubacha—Ghori’s slaves and successors/ claimants to his territories. Aibak married his daughter to Qubacha and thus brought him to his side; however, the threat from Yalduz continued. This is why Aibak always stayed in Lahore. He never got an opportunity to go to Delhi.

stem: Iltutmish appointed his first Subedar in Bihar to :
expl: Iltutmish captured Bihar Sharif and Barh, and near Teliyagarhi (close to the Rajmahal hills) a minor skirmish took place between Hisam-ud-din Aiwaz and the royal army. According to Minhaj, ultimately a treaty was concluded between the two sides. Iltutmish appointed Malik Jani as the Subedar of Bihar in place of Aiwaz.

stem: Who was the first Muslim ruler to formulate the 'Theory of Kingship' similar to the 'Theory of divine right of the kings'?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/ More than one of the above

expl: Balban was the first Muslim ruler who propounded the theory of kingship on the lines of the theory of divine right of kings. According to this, the Sultan is the representative of God on earth (niyabat-e-khudai), and his position comes after the Prophet. The king is zill-e-Allah or zill-e-ilahi, i.e., the reflection of God. He said to his son Bughra Khan—“The office of the Sultan is the living symbol of absolutism.”

stem: Which Delhi Sultan is known for adopting the 'blood and iron' policy?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: It is said about Balban that he adopted the policy of “blood and iron.” Two main features of Balban’s theory of kingship were: first, the post of the Sultan is bestowed by God, and second, the Sultan must be absolute. According to him, “The Sultan is God’s representative on earth (niyabat-e-khudai), and his position is after the Prophet. The Sultan receives inspiration and power from God. Therefore, common people or nobles have no right to criticize his actions.”

stem: Tughril Khan raised a standard of revolt during whose reign?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: An important revolt during Balban’s reign was the revolt of Tughril Khan. Balban had appointed Tughril Khan as the governor of Bengal, but he declared himself the independent ruler of Bengal, assumed the title of “Sultan Mugisuddin,” issued coins in his own name, and also had the khutba read in his name. To suppress Tughril’s revolt, Balban first sent an army under Amin Khan and thereafter under Bahadur, but both failed. Enraged, Balban advanced towards Bengal along with his son Bughra Khan, but Tughril fled after abandoning his capital. Ultimately, Tughril was captured and killed, and Balban appointed his son Bughra Khan as the iqtadar of Bengal.

stem: Who among the following introduced the Persian festival Nouruz in India?
expl: Ghiyas-ud-din Balban (1266–1287 A.D.) started the practice of celebrating the Iranian festival Nauroz in India. Nauroz is the Iranian New Year, also known as the Persian New Year. Balban also introduced the practices of sijda and paibos in his court, which were imitations of Persian tradition.
